Are there any ways to use known results about zero free regions to give \delta < 1? Or has that already been investigated?
I’ll check what the notes already investigated and how the known zero-free regions translate into the variance bound.

Yes, this has already been investigated. **Known zero-free regions improve the baseline, but they do not currently give a fixed global \(\delta<1\).**

The standard regions exclude zeros near \(1\) by a height-dependent margin, for example
\[
\Re\rho<1-\frac{c}{(\log|\Im\rho|)^{2/3}(\log\log|\Im\rho|)^{1/3}}.
\]
That margin tends to zero as the height increases. [Primary source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.06867).

Our [fixed-exponent theorem](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/manuscript.tex:73) requires a **constant margin at every height**:
\[
\mathcal V_g(X)=O(X^{2+\delta})
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\Re\rho\le\frac{1+\delta}{2}\quad\text{for every zero}.
\]
Thus even \(\delta=0.99\) would exclude every zero with real part above \(0.995\). Small coefficients at large heights do not bypass this: any forbidden zero leaves a nonzero pole in the response’s true Laplace transform.

The [earlier baseline investigation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations/sonin-critical-boundary/notes/subpower-milestones/01_baseline_and_exponent_budget_20261003.md) already transferred Johnston–Yang’s estimate to
\[
\mathcal V_g(X)\ll_g
X^3(\log X)^{3.602}
\exp\!\left[-0.3706\frac{(\log X)^{3/5}}{(\log\log X)^{1/5}}\right].
\]
This gives an effective exponent below \(3\) that approaches \(3\) as \(X\to\infty\); the saving cannot be fixed.

Known regions remain useful for sharper envelopes and finite-range bounds. A fixed global \(\delta<1\) would require additional information excluding zeros from a constant-width strip.
So if we could get any \delta<1 it would already be a result that would improve on zero free regions?

Yes. **Any fixed \(\delta<1\), proved globally for the actual prime response, would establish a substantial new zero-free result.**

Our equivalence would give
\[
\Re\rho\le 1-\frac{1-\delta}{2}
\]
for every nontrivial zero—a constant-width exclusion next to \(\Re s=1\).

Known unconditional zero-free regions have widths tending to zero with height, so this would improve them at sufficiently large heights. Even \(\delta=0.999999\) would give a new fixed strip.

It would not necessarily improve existing finite-height verification, and it would not prove RH. But the first fixed global \(\delta<1\) is already a major milestone.
